library(readr)

library(here)

tab <- function(name, ...) read_csv(here("outputs", "tables", name), show_col_types = FALSE, ...)
f2 <- function(x) sprintf("%.2f", x)
f3 <- function(x) sprintf("%.3f", x)
f4 <- function(x) sprintf("%.4f", x)
pct <- function(x) sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * x)

t01 <- tab("T01_dataset_summary.csv")
t02 <- tab("T02_cleaning_log.csv")
t03 <- tab("T03_hyperparameters.csv")
t04 <- tab("T04_cv_metrics.csv")
t05 <- tab("T05_test_metrics.csv")
t06 <- tab("T06_feature_importance.csv")
preds <- tab("test_predictions.csv", col_types = cols(objid = col_character(), .default = col_double()))

types <- cols(objid = col_character(), .default = col_double())
train <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "train.csv"), col_types = types)
test <- read_csv(here("data", "processed", "test.csv"), col_types = types)

# Figure captions written by the pipeline (outputs/figures/captions.md)
cap_lines <- readLines(here("outputs", "figures", "captions.md"), encoding = "UTF-8")
cap_lines <- cap_lines[startsWith(cap_lines, "- **F")]
caps <- setNames(sub("^- \\*\\*F[0-9]+:\\*\\* ", "", cap_lines),
                 sub("^- \\*\\*(F[0-9]+):.*$", "\\1", cap_lines))
cap <- function(id) paste0("Figure ", id, ". ", caps[[id]])
fig <- function(id) knitr::include_graphics(Sys.glob(here("outputs", "figures", paste0(id, "_*.png"))))

# Key quantities used in the text
n_raw <- t02$rows_before[t02$step == 1]
n_rule6 <- t02$rows_removed[t02$step == 6]
n_clean <- t02$rows_after[t02$step == 9]
z_row <- filter(t01, variable == "redshift")
ks <- ks.test(train$redshift, test$redshift)

learners <- c("M1_lm", "M2_knn", "M3_rf", "M4_svr")
cv_best <- t04 |> filter(model %in% learners) |> slice_min(rmse_mean, n = 1)
cv_base <- t04 |> filter(model == "M0_baseline")
te_best <- t05 |> filter(model %in% learners) |> slice_min(rmse, n = 1)
te_base <- t05 |> filter(model == "M0_baseline")
row05 <- function(id) filter(t05, model == id)
row04 <- function(id) filter(t04, model == id)

top <- t06 |> filter(rf_rank == 1)
neg <- preds |>
  tidyr::pivot_longer(all_of(learners), names_to = "model", values_to = "z_phot") |>
  filter(z_phot < 0)
FEATURES <- c("u_g", "g_r", "r_i", "i_z", "r")
outside_n <- sum(Reduce(`|`, lapply(FEATURES, \(f) test[[f]] < min(train[[f]]) | test[[f]] > max(train[[f]]))))
labels <- setNames(t05$label, t05$model)

# Learners whose whole 95% CI lies below the baseline RMSE (clear improvement)
clear_wins <- t05 |> filter(model %in% learners, rmse_hi < te_base$rmse) |> pull(label)
outlier_text <- if (te_best$eta == 0) "no catastrophic outliers" else
  paste0("catastrophic-outlier fraction ", pct(te_best$eta))

# Literature: SDSS photo-z with very large training sets reach sigma_NMAD ~ 0.02-0.03
LIT_SNMAD <- c(0.02, 0.03)
snmad_vs_lit <- if (te_best$sigma_nmad > LIT_SNMAD[2]) {
  "is larger than"
} else if (te_best$sigma_nmad >= LIT_SNMAD[1]) {
  "falls within"
} else {
  "is below"
}

# Include a generated markdown file, demoting its headings by `shift` levels
include_md <- function(lines, shift = 2) {
  lines <- sub("^(#+) ", paste0("\\1", strrep("#", shift), " "), lines)
  cat(lines, sep = "\n")
}
notes <- readLines(here("outputs", "tables", "interpretation_notes.md"), encoding = "UTF-8")
notes_section <- function(heading) {
  start <- which(notes == heading)
  rest <- which(startsWith(notes, "## ") & seq_along(notes) > start)
  end <- if (length(rest)) min(rest) - 1 else length(notes)
  notes[(start + 1):end]
}

# Abstract {-}

We predict the redshift of galaxies, a measure of their distance, from their
brightness in the five SDSS filters. The data are `r n_clean` galaxies from
the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (DR18) with spectroscopic redshifts between
`r f3(z_row$min)` and `r f3(z_row$max)`. They were cleaned with AI assistance
and split into `r nrow(train)` training and `r nrow(test)` test galaxies. Four
supervised models (linear regression, k-nearest neighbours, random forest and
support vector regression) were tuned by repeated cross-validation in R and
compared with a mean-prediction baseline. In cross-validation the best model
was `r cv_best$label` (RMSE `r f4(cv_best$rmse_mean)` vs `r f4(cv_base$rmse_mean)`
for the baseline). On the held-out test set the best model was
`r te_best$label` (RMSE `r f4(te_best$rmse)`, σ~NMAD~ `r f4(te_best$sigma_nmad)`,
`r outlier_text`). The colour g − r is by far the most important
predictor, and predicted redshift rises steadily with it. This is the
signature of the 4000 Å break moving through the g filter as galaxies recede.

# Introduction and physics background

## Redshift

Light from a receding galaxy is stretched to longer wavelengths:

$$ z = \frac{\lambda_{\text{obs}} - \lambda_{\text{emit}}}{\lambda_{\text{emit}}}, \qquad \lambda_{\text{obs}} = (1+z)\,\lambda_{\text{emit}}. $$

At low redshift, Hubble's law gives $v \approx cz = H_0 d$, so the redshift
measures distance.

## Spectroscopic versus photometric redshift

A **spectroscopic** redshift comes from the shift of spectral lines. It is
very precise but slow and expensive to obtain. A **photometric** redshift
estimates z from the brightness in a few broad filters. It is less precise
but works for billions of galaxies, which is essential for surveys such as
LSST, Euclid and DES. Galaxies that have both measurements let us *learn* the
mapping from photometry to redshift: a supervised regression problem.

## Why colours encode redshift: the 4000 Å break

Older stellar populations produce a sharp drop in galaxy spectra blueward of
4000 Å. As z increases, the break appears at $4000(1+z)$ Å and removes flux
from the bluer filter, so the colour (magnitude difference) between filters
changes. Figure F20 shows that, for the redshift range of this sample, the
break always lies inside the g band. We therefore expect **g − r** to redden
with redshift and to be the most informative feature. The r magnitude adds
distance information because, in a flux-limited sample, more distant galaxies
look fainter (inverse-square law).

```{r f20, fig.cap = cap("F20")}
fig("F20")
```

## Aim and hypotheses

Can a galaxy's colours predict its redshift? We test four hypotheses:

- **H1:** g − r is the most important predictor.
- **H2:** predicted redshift rises monotonically with g − r.
- **H3:** non-linear models (k-NN, random forest, SVR) beat linear regression.
- **H4:** all models beat the mean-prediction baseline.

# Data

## Acquisition

`r n_raw` random galaxies were retrieved from SDSS DR18 with a SkyServer SQL
query (`data/sql/sdss_query.sql`) by `R/01_acquire.R`. The query keeps
spectroscopically confirmed galaxies with reliable redshifts
(`zWarning = 0`), clean photometry, the Main Galaxy Sample flux limit
14 ≤ r ≤ 17.77, 0.01 < z < 0.5 and magnitude errors below 0.2. Magnitudes
are corrected for Milky Way dust (`dered_*`). The raw file is frozen and
recorded with an MD5 checksum in `data/raw/ACQUISITION.md`.

## AI-assisted inspection and cleaning

Following workflow step 2, an AI assistant (Claude Code) inspected the raw
data's structure, missing and sentinel values, duplicates, ranges and colour
outliers, then proposed cleaning rules. The student reviewed every rule. Each
rule logs its row counts (Table T02), and every AI interaction is recorded in
the appendix. The data contained no missing values, sentinels or duplicates.
The colour-outlier rule (median ± 5·MAD) removed `r n_rule6` galaxies that
were blue in all colours. The AI suggested keeping them as probably real
star-forming galaxies; the student chose to apply the planned rule. A random
sample of `r n_clean` galaxies (seed 42) forms the analysis set.

```{r t02}
knitr::kable(select(t02, step, rule, rows_before, rows_after, rows_removed),
             col.names = c("Step", "Rule", "Rows before", "Rows after", "Removed"),

```

# Methods

## Features and target

The target is the spectroscopic redshift. The features are the four colours
u − g, g − r, r − i, i − z and the r-band magnitude. Colours remove the overall
brightness and keep the shape of the spectrum, while r carries the
brightness–distance information.

## Train/test split

A stratified split on redshift (`caret::createDataPartition`, seed 42) gives
`r nrow(train)` training and `r nrow(test)` test galaxies. A two-sample KS test
finds no difference between their redshift distributions (D = `r f3(ks$statistic)`,
p = `r f3(ks$p.value)`, Figure F07). The test set was not used for any
training, tuning or preprocessing decision.

```{r f07, fig.cap = cap("F07")}
fig("F07")
```

## Models and tuning

All models use `redshift ~ u_g + g_r + r_i + i_z + r` and the **same** 25
resamples (5-fold cross-validation repeated 5 times) on the training set.
Hyperparameters were chosen by the lowest mean CV RMSE (Table T03). Centring
and scaling were fitted inside each training fold.

```{r t03}
knitr::kable(select(t03, label, parameter, search_grid, selected),
             col.names = c("Model", "Parameter", "Search grid", "Selected"),
             caption = "Table T03. Hyperparameter grids and selected values.")
```

## Metrics

With $\Delta z = (z_{\text{phot}} - z_{\text{spec}})/(1 + z_{\text{spec}})$ we
report RMSE, MAE, $R^2 = 1 - SS_{\text{res}}/SS_{\text{tot}}$, bias = mean(Δz),
the robust scatter $\sigma_{\text{NMAD}} = 1.4826 \times \text{median}(|\Delta z - \text{median}(\Delta z)|)$
and the catastrophic-outlier fraction η = fraction with |Δz| > 0.15. Test
metrics carry 95% percentile bootstrap confidence intervals (2000 resamples).

# Discussion: physics interpretation

## Which features matter and why

```{r t06}
knitr::kable(select(t06, label, rf_inc_mse, rf_rank, lm_std_coef, lm_ci_lo, lm_ci_hi, lm_rank),
             digits = 4,
             col.names = c("Feature", "RF %IncMSE", "RF rank", "LM std. coef.",
                           "LM CI low", "LM CI high", "LM rank"),
             caption = "Table T06. Feature importance: random-forest permutation importance and standardised linear-regression coefficients with 95% CIs.")
```

```{r f18, fig.cap = cap("F18")}
fig("F18")
```

```{r f19, fig.cap = cap("F19")}
fig("F19")
```

The random forest ranks `r top$label` first (%IncMSE `r f2(top$rf_inc_mse)`),
and the partial dependence (Figure F19) shows predicted redshift climbing
steadily with g − r. This is the behaviour expected from the 4000 Å break
moving redward through the g filter: the galaxy loses flux in g relative to r
and its g − r colour reddens. r − i correlates with z on its own (Figure F04)
but adds little once g − r is known, because the two colours are strongly
correlated (Figure F05).

```{r notes-importance, results = "asis"}
include_md(notes_section("## Feature importance (T06, F18)"))
```

## Hypotheses

```{r notes-hypotheses, results = "asis"}
include_md(notes_section("## Hypotheses (README §3.6)"))
```

## Where the models fail

Cross-validation ranks `r cv_best$label` first, but on the test set
`r te_best$label` is best. The difference comes from a few test galaxies whose
colours lie outside the range seen in training (`r outside_n` of
`r nrow(test)`). One of them has a red u − g but unusually blue g − r, r − i and
i − z. The linear model and the near-linear SVR extrapolate for it and predict
a **negative**, unphysical redshift (`r nrow(neg)` predictions below zero in
total). A random forest predicts averages of training redshifts and cannot
leave the training range, so it is more robust to such galaxies. Every model
also pulls the lowest- and highest-redshift galaxies towards the mean redshift
(Figure F15), a typical effect of a small training set.

With only `r nrow(test)` test galaxies the confidence intervals in Table T05
overlap strongly, so no model is clearly better than another on this test set.
The robust scatter σ~NMAD~ of `r f4(te_best$sigma_nmad)` (95% CI
`r f4(te_best$sigma_nmad_lo)`–`r f4(te_best$sigma_nmad_hi)`) `r snmad_vs_lit`
the ≈ `r LIT_SNMAD[1]`–`r LIT_SNMAD[2]` reported for SDSS photo-z trained on
hundreds of thousands of galaxies. With only `r nrow(train)` training
galaxies and a narrow redshift range this is encouraging, but the wide
interval means the comparison is not precise. The learning
curves (Figure F12) show the gap between training and test error for each
model as the training set grows.

```{r notes-physics, results = "asis"}
include_md(notes_section("## Physics of the sample"))
```

# Limitations

- **Small sample.** n = `r n_clean` is set by the assignment brief. Real
  photo-z work uses 10^5^–10^6^ training galaxies.
- **Small test set.** With `r nrow(test)` galaxies, metrics have wide
  confidence intervals and η can only change in steps of
  `r pct(1 / nrow(test))`.
- **Narrow redshift range.** The models are valid only for
  `r f3(z_row$min)` ≤ z ≤ `r f3(z_row$max)` and r ≤ 17.77. In this range the
  break never leaves the g band.
- **Very blue galaxies excluded.** The 5·MAD cleaning rule removed galaxies
  that are blue in every colour, so the models have not learned such objects.
- **Unphysical extrapolation.** The linear model and SVR can predict z < 0 for
  galaxies with colours outside the training range.
- **Unused information.** Magnitude errors were not used as weights or inputs.

# Conclusion

Five-band SDSS photometry predicts galaxy redshift better than a mean-value
baseline, even with only `r nrow(train)` training galaxies. On the test set
the best model, `r te_best$label`, reaches RMSE `r f4(te_best$rmse)` against
`r f4(te_base$rmse)` for the baseline.
`r n_beat <- sum(t05$rmse[t05$model %in% learners] < te_base$rmse); if (n_beat == length(learners)) "Every learner beats" else paste(n_beat, "of", length(learners), "learners beat")`
the baseline on the point estimate, but only `r if (length(clear_wins)) paste(clear_wins, collapse = ", ") else "no model"`
has a 95% confidence interval entirely below it, so with
`r nrow(test)` test galaxies the improvement is clear only for
`r if (length(clear_wins) == 1) "that model" else "those models"`. The models learn the physics: g − r,
which tracks the 4000 Å break moving through the g filter, dominates the
predictions, and predicted redshift rises monotonically with it. Smooth models
(linear regression, SVR) do best in cross-validation, while the random forest
is the most robust on unusual test galaxies because it cannot extrapolate to
unphysical values.
